Full legend, footnotes and disclosures on the desktop version.

Weights: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, relative importance, December 2025. Exposure tiers are editorial. Data 4 The People

What this does and does not say. "Diesel reaches 44.4% of the index" means diesel is an input cost somewhere inside categories making up 44.4% of the basket. It does not mean diesel drives 44.4% of inflation. Weighting each category by a rough estimate of how much of its delivered cost is actually diesel gives an embedded diesel cost of about 1.94% of the index — roughly 0.67× gasoline's entire direct weight, but spread across 60 categories instead of sitting in one box. Breadth is the claim here; that second number keeps it from being read as magnitude.

Method. Weights are the published relative importances from U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, taken at a single depth of the item tree so the 81 categories are mutually exclusive and sum to 100% — no category contains another. Motor fuel and household energy are split one level further so gasoline, diesel and heating oil are visible separately. Two rows in the published table carry the wrong indent level and are corrected before the tree is built; without that, the cut sums to 101.7% rather than 100%.

The tiers are editorial. The weights are BLS's. The exposure tiers and the narrative on each box are ours — a judgment about freight intensity, not a measured cost share, and not a BLS aggregate. Every assignment is listed with its reasoning in the project's exposure_tiers.py so it can be argued with one category at a time. Air travel is fuel-exposed but to jet fuel, and electricity and piped gas to their own fuels; both are deliberately excluded from the diesel total.

Source: Relative importance of components in the Consumer Price Indexes, December 2025, U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
